extracted.intended_audience: immigration applicants, advocates, practitioners, and DHS adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: DHS final rule explaining how officers should determine whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge, including definitions (receipt, government, household), the statutory minimum factors to consider, and how to weigh evidence (recency, duration, totality of circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Health (including long-term institutionalization at government expense)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider past or current long-term institutionalization at government expense under the health factor as part of the totality of the circumstances. Commitment to a psychiatric facility pursuant to judicial order pending or after a finding of incompetence to stand trial may be considered if the underlying condition is identified on Form I-693. Commitment to a facility, rather than prison, resulting from a criminal proceeding would not be considered long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will look at recency and duration of long-term institutionalization. Receipt of Medicaid for the purpose of obtaining preventive services or treatment for COVID-19 will not be considered. For children, DHS can consider evidence that the child's condition is not permanent, can be managed through home- and community-based services (HCBS) rather than long-term institutionalization, or that the child was/ is institutionalized in violation of their rights. DHS treats long-term institutionalization as potentially probative of likely future primary dependence but will include it only as one element in the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal incarceration (not considered under public charge)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is not taking into consideration current or past incarceration for a crime in a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal activity may separately subject a noncitizen to criminal grounds of inadmissibility even if public charge is not found. Distinguish incarceration (not considered) from institutional commitment for medical/psychiatric reasons (may be considered in limited circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of public benefits — definition of 'receipt'
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of public benefits occurs when a public benefit‑granting agency provides public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense to a noncitizen, where the noncitizen is listed as a beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying for a benefit on one's own behalf or on behalf of another, receiving benefits on behalf of another, approval for future receipt, or assisting another with the application does not itself constitute receipt. However, evidence of approval for future receipt may be considered in the totality of the circumstances as probative of likely future receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded benefits from consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider receipt of, or certification or approval for future receipt of, public benefits not referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) or (c). The rule explicitly lists examples such as Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) or other nutrition programs, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), Medicaid (other than for long-term use of institutional services under section 1905(a) of the Social Security Act), housing benefits, any benefits related to immunizations or testing for communicable diseases, or other supplemental or special-purpose benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS added explicit regulatory text (8 CFR 212.22(a)(3)) to reduce uncertainty and chilling effects; these benefits will not be considered in public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of dependents' receipt (not considered)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider a noncitizen's dependent's receipt of public benefits in a public charge inadmissibility determination; DHS will only consider benefits received by the noncitizen applying for the immigration benefit as a named beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although prior policies allowed consideration of a dependent's receipt, DHS declines to adopt that approach here because the statute does not require it and because DHS expects it to be rare that a noncitizen subsists primarily on dependents' benefits. DHS emphasizes this limitation to reduce incentives for disenrollment of eligible dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government — scope of entities whose benefits may be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is defined to mean any Federal, State, Tribal, territorial, or local government entity or entities of the United States; public cash assistance and long-term institutionalization provided by these entities may be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS declined to limit consideration to Federal programs only, reasoning that excluding State/Tribal/territorial/local benefits would unfairly distinguish recipients and would be inconsistent with Congressional intent and historical practice (including State 'deeming' provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Household — definition used for family status and assets/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: A noncitizen's household is defined as: (1) the alien; (2) the alien's spouse, if physically residing with the alien; (3) if physically residing with the alien, the alien's parents, the alien's unmarried siblings under 21 years of age, and the alien's children as defined in section 101(b)(1) of the INA; (4) any other individuals (including a spouse or child as defined in section 101(b)(1) of the Act not physically residing with the alien) who are listed as dependents on the alien's federal income tax return; and (5) any other individual(s) who list the alien as a dependent on their federal income tax return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS adopted this simpler definition rather than the 2019 Final Rule's threshold-based (50 percent support) approach to avoid burdensome quantification and potential unfairness to larger or informal-support households. The definition is intended to provide officers clarity about whose resources are considered in assessing family status and assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers are required by statute to consider, at a minimum, a noncitizen's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills. Where required, consideration also includes the Affidavit of Support under section 213A of the INA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute does not prescribe how to treat these factors positively or negatively, nor specific weights. DHS will not codify exhaustive evidentiary requirements for each factor; instead officers will assess these factors in the totality of the circumstances. The rule states that none of these statutory minimum factors other than lack of a sufficient Affidavit of Support (if required) should be the sole criterion for determining public charge inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances approach and subregulatory guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will make public charge determinations based on the totality of a noncitizen's circumstances and plans to issue subregulatory guidance to officers that includes an empirical analysis of how the identified factors may affect likelihood of becoming primarily dependent on the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance will inform but not dictate outcomes, will address recency/duration and other relevant evidence, will be informed by best-available data, is to be issued prior to the rule's implementation, and may be periodically updated to promote consistency and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting and examples (recency, duration, proportion of income)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should consider the recency and duration of benefit receipt and the proportion of the applicant's income coming from public cash assistance when weighing evidence. The rule provides hypotheticals: e.g., long-ago, short-term, small-portion benefits are less probative; extended current receipt comprising most income, with little other resources, is more probative of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider combinations of factors (age, health, family status, assets/resources, education/skills, past/current receipt of public cash assistance or long-term institutionalization, and a sufficient Affidavit of Support where required) and empirical guidance to reach a totality-based determination. Recency, duration, and repeat institutionalization increase probative value regarding likely future primary dependence.
